From Catherine

​Support True the Vote’s work​

Hi Friend —

Keeping up with the news these days means constantly sorting through what’s true, what’s distorted, and what’s been made up entirely ... it’s exhausting, but necessary.

This week, we learned that fabricated polls have defined this season's national election coverage — the very numbers relied upon to tell the country who’s winning were bogus.

In election season, polling can build or break momentum. Polls drive headlines, influence donations, and shape whether people believe their vote will matter.

That’s why this week’s revelation was so consequential. Wedgewood Polls, a provider of 15 polls included in the New York Times’ polling tracker, admitted that all but one of its polls had been fabricated. Invented numbers were presented as the voice of the American people, with the credibility of the Times behind them.

Even legitimate polling faces challenges in today's culture. Pew’s telephone response rate fell from 36% in 1997 to 6% in 2018, and researchers find growing evidence that Republicans are less likely than Democrats to participate.

The industry’s own review found that late polls overstated Democratic margins by 3.1 points in 2016, 4.6 in 2020, and 2.7 in 2024. Recent midterm polls performed better, but the record calls for humility. Instead, uncertain numbers become confident declarations about who’s winning and who should give up.

For those of us who cherish liberty, pessimism can begin to feel like realism. We value honesty. We keep our word. We expect fair dealing. Watching those standards violated again and again wears on us. Our confidence suffers, and eventually, expecting the worst can feel like the only sensible position.

But that is a conclusion we need to examine, too.

The dishonesty is real, but it does not mean that goodness is scarce, that we stand alone, or that our efforts are futile. A steady diet of betrayal and dysfunction has distorted understandings of our country and of one another.

We must bring discernment to everything. Don't be too quick to believe the hype. What supports it? What does it leave out? Have we mistaken what dominates the headlines for what defines the country?

Talk to your neighbors. Spend time in your community. A conversation across the kitchen table is real. So are the good people quietly keeping their promises, helping others, and doing their part. We have a part in strengthening that goodness, too.

And voting is real. The process is imperfect and protecting it takes work — your participation is critical.

We’ve added a way to check your early voting activity through Scan. Check. Protect., including whether your ballot has been recorded in the data the states release. Updates follow state reporting schedules; recorded activity does not confirm inclusion in the final count.

Visit ScanCheckProtect.org, check your record, check activity at your address, and encourage someone else to do the same.

Last week, I wrote about answering the call: “Here am I. Send me.” That call still stands. Learning something difficult, like fraud in polling, changes our understanding of what we face. It doesn’t diminish our ability — or our responsibility — to take a stand and make a difference.

God has given us minds to reason, neighbors to love, work to do, and infinite reasons to keep hope alive.

Never quit. Ephesians 6 and Isaiah 6:8 FTW!

Ever onward —

P.S. Looking for a clearer read on the polls? Our friends at Onward Media built People's Poll, a fresh take on polling. It tracks every published 2026 Senate, governor and House poll and links each one to its source, so you can check the numbers yourself. Take a look at peoplespoll.com.

Help us keep going

Your gift helps True the Vote keep tools like Scan. Check. Protect. available to voters.

Give today

A message from someone you know moves people to vote in a way mass campaign messages can't.

  • Texts from friends boost turnout. In a Columbia University study, a text from a friend raised turnout 8.3 percentage points. Mass automated texts average less than half a point.
  • Small margins decide big elections. Just 187 votes decided a seat in Congress in 2024. Reaching even a few friends makes a real difference.
  • Connection and a plan. What works is a friendly nudge from someone you trust, plus help making a real plan: when, where and how you'll vote.

Simple ways to help your seven: share their polling place, send date reminders, or offer a ride or a hand.

Get started at 7votes.org

Sources: Schein, Green et al., Columbia University, friend-to-friend texting in the 2018 midterms; 2024 U.S. House results.

In other news ...

Placeholder Votes..?

Questions are mounting over alleged discrepancies between early-voting check-ins and voter history records in Georgia. Could missing records indicate processing errors, or something more serious? Without timely, verifiable check-in records, the public is left asking questions. Election transparency shouldn't require guesswork.

​Read the Post​

North Carolina: One Voter. Multiple Records?

A new complaint alleges 3,674 sets of duplicate or triplicate voter registrations in North Carolina. The state acknowledges ongoing cleanup efforts, but the watchdog group wants systemic fixes. Because cleaning voter rolls shouldn't be a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

​Read More​

Don't forget! You can check your own voter registration record and your activity right now. Visit scancheckprotect.org and take three minutes to:

  1. Confirm your current record is accurate — your name, address, and status.
  2. See if your early vote was recorded — check back if your state hasn't reported yet.
  3. Verify that your address isn't being used as a voter trap house — after you pull up your record, check your current address and confirm you recognize anyone else who may be registered at your residence.
  4. Check the rolls in states where you used to live — old registrations often linger for years after you've moved, sometimes without your knowledge.
  5. Tell us what you found. Good or bad, we want to hear from you — and if something looks off, we're here to help you fix it.

item.title: Stop the Spread (It's not what you think)
item.description:
​
​

Discouragement is spreading. Here’s the cure, and it starts with people you already know.

​

In this newsletter:

  • Why “why bother?” is the most dangerous message of 2026
  • Your three-minute assignment: seven people
  • Hawaii and Wyoming: we need you!

Hi Friend,

Something is spreading across America, and it isn’t just political division.

It’s a shrug.

It’s the text from a friend that says, “What’s the point?” It’s the neighbor who’s “sitting this one out.” It’s the quiet belief that the outcome is already decided and showing up is a waste of time.

In 2020, Americans were told: Trust the system. Stop asking questions.

In 2026, the message is: Why bother voting at all?

Different messages — same destination: Surrender.

Yeah...we don't do that.

For years, we’ve urged Americans to ask hard questions, examine the records, learn election law, and hold officials accountable. None of that matters if we give up the one responsibility that belongs to every eligible voter:

Showing up.

Stop the Spread. VOTE.

Let's take their viral (no pun intended) message and use it for good.

America is worth showing up for. Not because everything is perfect, or because every question has been answered. It’s because a republic can’t preserve itself. It requires participation.

​Watch this short video. Send it to someone who’s discouraged. Remind them that sitting out doesn’t fix what’s broken.

Your assignment: Seven people.

The people you know won’t be moved by one more political ad. They might be moved by you.

A text from a friend boosts turnout 8.3 points. A mass campaign text? Less than half a point. In 2024, 187 votes decided a House seat. Your seven matter.

That’s why we built 7Votes.org:

  1. Visit 7Votes.org.
  2. Choose seven people you know.
  3. Send each one a personal invitation to make a plan to vote.

It takes about three minutes. It’s free and nonpartisan. You don’t have to persuade strangers. You just have to reach seven people who already trust you.

Wyoming and Hawaii: We need you!

Forty-eight states are lit up with TTV citizens learning together, sharing information, and strengthening their communities.

Two are still dark: Wyoming. Hawaii.

If you live in either state, raise your hand. If you know someone who does, send them our way. Let’s finish the map.

Here’s what to do next:

  • Watch and share Stop the Spread.
  • ​Invite seven people through 7Votes.org.
  • Help us light up Wyoming and Hawaii.

Election Day is 12 days away. The clock is running, and the answer isn’t another argument.

It’s action.

Fear can be contagious, but courage spreads the same way: one person, one conversation, one invitation at a time.

Stop the spread. Start with seven.

God bless you, and God bless America.

Ever onward —

"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today." - Genesis 50:20

item.title: What I saw in the ER last night
item.description:
| Read Online​

​

Hi Friend,

Last night I took my son to the ER.

We’re okay now. But we were there for more than eight hours, and what I saw in that local hospital stayed with me.

Part of it was just being in a children’s ER. Watching kids hurt and parents frightened is hard. But that wasn’t all of it. Looking around that waiting room, I realized I was surrounded by the very people we’re fighting for: the underprivileged and the undersupported, the families who have been made promise after promise by a system that keeps failing them.

These are the people big government says it’s protecting. Too often, it’s the people big government takes advantage of. For far too long it has kept them dependent and overlooked, and kept telling them their voice doesn’t matter.

Many of them don’t know it’s happening. They’re tired. They’re working, waiting, and holding their families together. They have no time to read the fine print or follow the headlines. They’ve been told for so long that the system will take care of them that they’ve stopped expecting anything else.

I sat there holding my son, and I felt two things at once.

The first was heartbreak. If you stop and actually see what’s going on around us, it breaks your heart.

The second was anger. I wasn’t angry at the people in that room. I was angry for them. These families were promised so much and given so little, and the system that made those promises is still counting on them to stay home, stay quiet, and stay tired.

But every strong emotion carries a signal. Heartbreak tells you what matters. Anger tells you something is wrong and needs to change. You can act on it, or you can let it pass.

I don’t want to let it pass.

Over the next two weeks, you’ll hear plenty of noise. Over the next two weeks, it will be increasingly more difficult to hold on to our compassion. The polls will swing back and forth, because drama is built into how polling works. The headlines will pile on one crisis after another, and much of it will seem designed to make ordinary people feel like showing up won’t matter.

Don’t believe it.

When you invest in Mobilize A Million, you’re investing in the little guy. You’re investing in the mom in that waiting room who has been let down again and again and doesn’t know her vote is just as powerful as anyone’s. You’re investing in the dad working a double shift who never got a reminder to check his registration. You’re investing in the families who have stopped believing anyone is looking out for them.

That’s who this is for. It isn’t for politicians or pundits. It’s for the people in the waiting room.

Election Day is November 3. Until then, our team is working to make sure everyday citizens know their registration is accurate, know where and how to vote, and know their voice counts.

​Check your registration and send it to three people you love →​

​Stand with the little guy. Give today →​

I left that hospital exhausted and grateful my son is okay. I was still a little heartbroken and still a little angry. I’ve decided to put both feelings to work. The people who have been failed the longest deserve to be seen, counted, and heard.

Let’s not fail them now.

For Freedom,

Sarah

item.title: Here Am I. Send Me. — A Birthday Lesson
item.description:
| Read Online​

From Catherine

Hi Friend —

Sometimes a few words from someone you love stay with you longer than you expect.

Tuesday was Gregg’s birthday. A member of my family sent him a text that I’ve been thinking about ever since:

Happy Birthday! I ran across a bible verse that made me think of you. It’s Isaiah 6:8.

Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?’ And I said, ‘Here am I. Send me!’

I strive to be that guy. You actually are that guy.

What a thing to say to someone: “I strive to be that guy. You actually are that guy.”

And it’s true about Gregg. In ways seen and unseen, he is always ready to serve. Whatever the assignment, whatever the personal cost, he goes.

But as I reread that message, I began to think about what those words ask of the rest of us.

“Here am I. Send me.”

If you regularly read these letters, you know my familiar closing: “Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW”—for the win. I’ve signed off that way for years, and I still mean every word.

Paul’s call in Ephesians to put on the full armor of God reminds us that readiness to serve is not merely a matter of personality or willpower. We are called to stand firm in faith, truth, righteousness, peace, and prayer, prepared for whatever God places before us.

But lately, I think we’re in an Isaiah 6:8 moment, too. A moment that asks each of us what we are willing to do with the faith we profess and the freedom we’ve been given.

I look around and wonder how so much has changed in our country, in our culture. I worry about what our children are inheriting. Some days, it’s hard to know what to believe or where to begin.

Then I remember: our time here is not an accident. We have work to do.

These midterm elections will help determine how much harder that work becomes. The choice matters. If we preserve liberty, we preserve the ability to correct our mistakes, challenge our leaders, and keep working toward something better. Every freedom we surrender makes that work harder.

Honest elections. Safe communities. An immigration system that works. The opportunity to build a life through our own efforts. A government that respects its constitutional limits. These are reasonable expectations of a free country, and we should have the confidence to insist on them.

America has come through bitter divisions and dangerous days before. Each generation has had to decide what it would preserve, what it would repair, and what it would pass on. Now that responsibility belongs to us.

By 2028, I believe advances in artificial intelligence will have changed daily life in ways we are only beginning to understand. As technology grows more powerful, we will need to be even more deliberate about protecting human freedom, human judgment, and our connections to one another.

Which brings me back to that birthday text—and to 7 Votes.

We do not have to know everything the future holds to accept responsibility for what we can do today.

Start with seven people you know. Reach out. Help them make a plan to vote. Their 7 Votes profile gives them a place to check their registration, find where to vote, and get local voting information. Stay in touch through Election Day.

There is something powerful in that simple act of connection. A friend hears from a friend. Someone who feels forgotten knows they matter. Someone who might have stayed home has a plan—and someone encouraging them to follow through.

We strengthen our country through those relationships. We keep our humanity by caring for one another. And we defend freedom by exercising it and helping others do the same.

For these next two weeks, let’s invite everyone we can to vote. Let’s speak plainly about what freedom makes possible. Let’s give people a reason to believe their participation matters, and help them act on it.

There is still so much good in this country. So much worth protecting. So much we can do.

The question before us is familiar: “Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?”

Let’s answer it together.

Here am I. Send me.

Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 AND Isaiah 6:8 FTW! God will never leave nor forsake us — let’s gooooo!

Ever onward —

P.S. — If you can support our work, please do. We are pushing hard!​

​7 Votes is active in 48 states with over 700 organizers and tens of thousands of voters are being reached. Those numbers will grow exponentially by Election Day — and it will make a difference!  This year’s races will be close!! Every vote counts! Please support the work if you can. It allows us to move faster and do more.​

Stand With True the Vote

We can't do this without you — and we wouldn't want to.

Thank you for your support!

Another week ...

Texas: The Glitch That Keeps on Giving

A DPS software failure left more than 8,000 Lubbock County voter registration records in limbo, part of a statewide problem affecting at least 591,000 records. The county has since cleared its original backlog, but another processing error has surfaced. Early voting begins October 19. Apparently, the software didn't get the memo.

Read the Article

Oklahoma: Registration Deadline Meets Error Message

On the final day to register for November's election, Oklahoma's online voter registration system malfunctioned, leaving some applicants staring at error messages instead of confirmations. Officials expect minimal impact. We'd still like to know how many eligible voters were affected.

Read More

California: 650,000 Ballots Headed for Destruction

Riverside County plans to destroy approximately 650,000 Proposition 50 ballots previously seized by Sheriff Chad Bianco during an investigation. The county says state law requires their destruction following a California Supreme Court ruling against the seizure. Bianco warns potential evidence could be lost. And the destruction? Behind closed doors.

Read More

Texas: 1.8 Million in Suspense

Texas's voter suspense list has climbed to nearly 1.8 million ahead of early voting. Suspense status doesn't automatically mean a voter is ineligible, but it does signal that registration information needs attention. With Election Day approaching, checking your record isn't optional homework anymore.

Read More

Michigan: 37 Ballots. One Reversed Election.

Nearly a year after Hamtramck's mayoral election, officials finally counted 37 disputed absentee ballots. The result? A race originally decided by 11 votes now shows the challenger ahead by 12. Thirty-seven ballots changed the outcome. Tell us again why every ballot doesn't matter.

Read More

Detroit: How Many Applications Does One Voter Need?

New reporting alleges multiple voter registration applications tied to Detroit records, raising questions about duplicate submissions, verification, and safeguards against misuse. What do the underlying documents reveal—and what action have election officials taken?

Read More

California: Ballots, Ballots Everywhere

Tulare County is facing questions over duplicate mail ballots sent to voters. A printing or mailing mistake is one thing. Explaining how duplicate ballots are tracked and prevented from being counted twice is another. Voters deserve both answers.

Read More

Michigan: DOJ Enters the Fight

​

The Department of Justice has reportedly filed a statement of interest in Michigan election litigation. The filing could bring federal legal arguments into an already contentious dispute. The key question is what position the DOJ is taking—and what it means for the case.

item.title: Someone you know needs a reason to show up and vote
item.description:
Someone you know needs a reason to show up and vote. Give them one.

Dear friend,

How many people in your life would take a call from you, read your text, or listen when you said, “This matters”?

Your sister. A neighbor. A friend from church. Someone who’s frustrated enough to sit this election out.

You can’t make their decisions for them. But you can remind them that their voice matters—and help them make a plan to use it.

That’s why we built 7 Votes.

It’s a simple, free way to turn “somebody should do something” into something each of us can do.

Pick seven people you know. Each day, 7 Votes gives you a short message you can send in seconds. Your friends get a link to check their registration, make a voting plan, and follow through.

A little encouragement. A practical next step. From someone they trust.

You don’t need a platform or a big following. You already have a place to start.

And people are starting.

Those numbers represent people reaching into their own circles and saying, “Let’s do our part.” Every invitation is a chance to bring someone into the process who might otherwise sit it out.

Help us keep it growing.

7 Votes is free, and we intend to keep it that way. We don’t sell personal information, collect contact lists, or ask how anyone votes.

item.title: 20 Days. One Election. Lawmakers on the Ballot.
item.description:
| Read Online​

​

You can't vote on every bill. But you can vote for who does.

​

Key Highlights:

  • The people who wrote these laws are on your ballot. This year 6,139 state legislative seats are up for election, along with every U.S. House seat and about a third of the Senate.
  • The SAVE Act didn’t pass. The SAVE Kansas Act did. What Congress debated compared with what states actually enacted.
  • Already law for Nov. 3: new citizenship checks in Kansas and Mississippi, and narrower backup ID options in Kentucky.
  • Passed, but not yet in effect: Florida starts in January. Tennessee’s citizenship-check portal is due by 2028.
  • Three things to check in the next 20 days and how you can help with 7Votes.

​

Hi Friend,

The SAVE Act never became law, and there is still so much conversation around this. But let's not forget that states took matters into their hands — and even more importantly — the people writing the laws are on the ballot in this upcoming midterm election.

For more than a year, Washington has argued over how citizenship should be verified and what voters should show at the polls. The bills passed the House, stalled in the Senate, and became headlines.

Meanwhile, state legislatures passed their own laws, and several are already in effect.

20 days until Election Day. The laws we debate are not always the laws we vote under. The difference comes down to who has the votes.

You’re voting for lawmakers.

In April, the Kansas House voted 84–41 to override a veto of the SAVE Kansas Act. It needed exactly 84 votes. One fewer, and the override would have failed.

On November 3, all 125 Kansas House seats are up for election.

Think about that. A law can hinge on a single vote in a state legislature. And voters get to decide who occupies those seats next.

This isn't just happening in Kansas.

Across the country, Americans will elect state lawmakers who will consider legislation affecting voter registration, identification requirements, ballot procedures, and election oversight.

And in Washington, every U.S. House seat and approximately one-third of the Senate will be on the ballot. Those elected will help determine what happens next with federal election legislation, including proposals like the SAVE Act.

The laws don't write themselves. People write them. And voters choose those people.

November 3 isn't just about who holds office. It's about who will have a say in the laws governing future elections.

The laws we debated

The SAVE proposals would have required documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote. The expanded SAVE America Act added photo ID. Neither is federal law.

Citizenship is already required to vote in federal elections. What varies is how each state checks it. That’s where the action has been.

Congress

​H.R. 22 — SAVE Act: Requires proof of U.S. citizenship to register for federal elections.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Passed the House 220–208 in April 2025. Still awaiting Senate action.
  • What's next: No vote scheduled. The bill expires January 3, 2027, if not enacted.

​H.R. 7296 — SAVE America Act: Adds photo ID requirements for voting in person and by mail, along with proof of citizenship to register.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: The House approved the SAVE America legislation 218–213 in February 2026. The Senate has not passed it.
  • What's next: No vote scheduled.

​H.R. 7008 — Stop Insider Trading Act: Combines restrictions on congressional stock trading with a federal voter photo ID requirement.

  • TTV Position: Watch
  • Status: Passed the House 232–198 in July. A Senate vote to advance the legislation failed 53–47 on September 30.
  • What's next: No vote scheduled.

Why the 53–47 vote stands out: Even though a majority voted to advance the legislation, it fell short of the 60 votes generally needed to end debate in the Senate.

The laws we have

Washington is still debating federal election requirements, but states haven't been waiting. Some passed new laws this year, others are preparing changes for future elections, and several proposals remain unresolved. Here's where things stand as November 3 approaches.

Kansas — HB 2437: SAVE Kansas Act: Requires twice-yearly citizenship checks of voter rolls using the federal SAVE database, with county follow-up on flagged records.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Legislature overrode the governor’s veto in April. In effect since July 1.
  • What’s next: A possible legal challenge; no lawsuit date confirmed.

Kentucky — HB 139: Voter ID and Roll Maintenance: Tightens accepted voter ID options, ends poll-worker vouching, and permits federal data checks for voter eligibility.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Legislature overrode the governor’s veto in April. In effect since July 15.
  • What’s next: November 3 is the first general election under the new law.

Mississippi — SB 2588: SHIELD Act: Requires citizenship checks for voter registration applications, with additional documentation when eligibility cannot be verified.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Signed April 1. In effect since July 1.
  • What’s next: November 3 is the first general election under the law.

The laws on the way

Passed, but their new requirements won’t apply this November.

Florida — HB 991: Citizenship Verification: Requires additional proof of citizenship for certain voter registrations and updates.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Signed April 1; challenged in federal court.
  • What’s next: Scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027, subject to litigation.

Tennessee — HB 2185: SAVE Database Portal: Authorizes an electronic portal for citizenship verification using the federal SAVE database.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Enacted April 2026.
  • What’s next: Portal development deadline is January 1, 2028.

Still pending

Proposed legislation that has not become law.

Michigan — HB 4765: Proof of Citizenship and Voter ID: Would require proof of citizenship for new voter registrations and identification to vote.

  • TTV Position: Support
  • Status: Passed the House in April; awaiting Senate committee action.
  • What’s next: No vote scheduled. The bill could still advance this year.

Three weeks. Three things to know.

  1. Know your registration. Check your voter record, address, and status through your state’s official election system at ScanCheckProtect.org. Don’t wait until Election Day to find a problem.
  2. Know your ballot. Look up which offices, candidates, and measures you’ll be voting on, and what each office actually does.
  3. Know your state’s rules — this year’s version. Check your ID requirements, polling place, hours, and voting options.

Connect your 7.

Since the launch of LegiTrack, you have witnessed the good, the bad, the ugly, and the close calls.

We. must. vote.

​Join 7Votes. It's free and nonpartisan.

The idea is simple: start with 7 people, help them make a plan to vote, and encourage them to reach 7 more. Even if you’re already planning to vote, you can help make a difference.

Legislation in this nation is at stake. Don't sit this election out.

Don’t confuse frustration with helplessness.

You don’t have to wait for Congress. You can read the laws, check the legislative record, verify your registration, and ask your election officials questions.

You can vote and ensure the laws your state needs are passed — even when it's right on the edge.

See what passed, what’s pending, and what changes next in your state at LegiTrack.org.

We spend all year watching their votes. Now it's our turn.

Ever onward -

187 votes decided a seat in Congress. Your seven could be the start of the next margin.

item.title: Do. Not. Give. Up. Please read.
item.description:
| Read Online​

From Catherine

Hi Friend —

The headlines are enough to give you whiplash.

A few years ago, questioning election security got you labeled a conspiracy theorist. Now, the failures you were told didn’t exist are making headlines.

It’s becoming nearly impossible to know what to believe.

I’m weary of it. I suspect you are, too. And if we feel this way after years of paying close attention, imagine how it feels for someone just trying to make sense of the headlines.

For years, legitimate questions have been dismissed as "crazy conspiracies", and citizens — including many of us — have been discredited simply for reporting what we found or experienced firsthand.

Now we’re facing a tsunami of headlines about the very failures they spent years dismissing. What the mockbird media on both sides of the aisle buried a few years ago, they broadcast now* — and I believe the calculation is political: overwhelm you, discourage you, and convince you there’s no point in trying.

Do not let them get in your head.

Our election process has serious problems, but sitting out will solve none of them.

Believe me, I understand the anger. I’ve spent years in this fight. I know what it costs to keep going when institutions fail you, when the story gets twisted, when accountability always seems to be somebody else’s responsibility.

But I also know this: withdrawing leaves the decisions to whoever remains. And we are making progress! Yes, it's slower and far more difficult than in should be, but we are still moving forward!.

So - we have to vote. And we have to document failures, demand answers, and stay engaged at every level after the votes are counted.

Do not back down. We can still correct course. Do. Not. Give. Up.

And because you deserve more than another email telling you to keep fighting, we’ve built something to help. 🇺🇸 😊 🇺🇸

It’s called 7 Votes. And it puts a little encouragement, connection, and even fun back into showing up at the polls!

At 7votes.org, you choose seven people you know and help them follow through on voting.

Think about who those people might be. The friend who’s had enough. The neighbor who doesn’t think one vote matters. The family member who needs someone they trust to say, “I hear you. I’m frustrated, too. Let’s see this through.”

Be that person!

7 Votes makes it simple:

  • Pick your seven. Add their first names or choose them from your contacts.
  • Send a note. The app helps draft messages about checking registration, making a voting plan, and voting. Make them your own and send them from your phone.
  • Follow through together. Your friends mark their progress through a link, so you can see who’s ready and who could use another reminder.

There’s a leaderboard, too, because a little friendly competition never hurts. And when your seven invite seven more, you can watch your reach grow.

It’s free. It’s nonpartisan. Nobody asks how anyone votes, just encourages your family and friends TO vote!

With 23 days until Election Day, here is something you can do today.

Let the people you know hear from someone they trust. Give them a reason to stay engaged. Help them take the next step.

We have too much worth fighting for to sit this out.

Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW!

Ever onward —

*From Above: To be clear, more headlines do not mean the media has suddenly committed to finding the truth about our elections. We’re seeing coverage of process failures and stories that hint at larger political scandals. But the biggest questions—including those we’ve spent years pursuing—are still radioactive.

Still, I’m glad these issues are getting attention. The problems are real, even when I believe the decision to cover them is politically calculated. Every honest report gives the public a chance to understand more and demand better.

And who knows? Maybe following a few uncomfortable facts will help some journalists find their way back to their own integrity.

I’m not holding my breath. But a girl can dream.

Stand With True the Vote

We can't do this without you — and we wouldn't want to.

Thank you for your support!

What a week ...

Shasta Co, CA: "The Shred"

On October 3, the state of California sent a shredding truck to Shasta County to destroy ballots and other election materials from 2024 that were being preserved for a federal investigation.

Shasta County deserves answers. So does every American voter.

Watch the Documentary

Louisiana: "Human Error"

If there wasn't ever a reason to verify your record, now you have one after 67 thousand records in Louisiana were erroneously switched to "inactive". They call it human error. We call it a failed system.

Read More

Colorado: A Taxing Problem

Approximately 800k CO voters received ballots asking them to approve $580m in debt and a tax projected to raise $295m annually. The problem? They don't live in the district and weren't eligible to vote on it.

Just another thing that "never happens"...

Read More

Georgia: $107 Million Later… Now What?

GA spent $107m on Dominion voting equipment in 2020. Six years later, lawmakers are considering replacements while taxpayers are still paying off the original purchase.

Wasn't this the system used in what officials called the “most secure election ever”?

Read More

Georgia: The Hypocrisy

The Secretary of State knowingly shares GA residents voting AND driver's license data with a non-government entity but refuses to share it with the federal government...yup. See page 11 from ERIC's own bylaws.

See the Post

Circa 2007, Texas? Really?

Nearly 20 years ago, a State Auditor's report found that over half of surveyed county voter-registration offices said the TEAM system wasn't allowing them to do their jobs effectively.

The problems have been documented for years. Why haven't they been resolved?

Read More

San Francisco: So Much for Measures to Limit Mail Voting

San Francisco mailed more than 500k ballots. Now some are arriving TORN.

More mail ballots, more opportunities for things to go wrong. Voters deserve better.

Read More

Georgia: Double the Absentee Fun

Athens-Clarke County officials blame a duplicate mailing list sent to the printer.

But here's the question: How did 1,154 duplicate ballots get mailed in the first place?

Read article

One more plug for 7 Votes! Join us! it's fun!

Seven People. Seven Votes. One Powerful Difference.

​7Votes.org is a new, free, nonpartisan initiative from True the Vote Now that makes it easy to connect with seven of your contacts, encourage them to participate, and help them get to the polls. We'll provide the tools and resources. You bring the personal connection.

Elections are decided by those who show up, and sometimes just a handful of votes make all the difference.

Are you sure you're registered?

You can check your own voter registration record right now. Visit scancheckprotect.org and take three minutes to:

  1. Confirm your current record is accurate — your name, address, and status.
  2. Verify that your address isn't being used as a voter trap house — after you pull up your record, check your current address and confirm you recognize anyone else who may be registered at your residence.
  3. Check the rolls in states where you used to live — old registrations often linger for years after you've moved, sometimes without your knowledge.
  4. Tell us what you found. Good or bad, we want to hear from you — and if something looks off, we're here to help you fix it.

Tools for Your Toolkit

You weren't meant to do this alone. Find your community, your tools, your purpose.

Become a Member

Stay ahead of the legislation shaping your elections and know when it's time to act.

Join LegiTrack

Grounded in Truth

A weekly word from the TTV team. Want one every day? Join us in TTV Now.​

Father,

Today we ask You to give us hearts that are willing to listen and the courage to act when You call us to move. Give us discernment to recognize what is right, wisdom to know what needs to be done, and boldness to take the next step in obedience. Keep us from allowing fear or the comfort of standing still to keep us from the purpose You have placed before us. Help us to keep moving forward instead of hesitating even when we cannot see the entire path ahead. Give us the faith to follow where You are leading us. And hearts that are ready to say, “Here I am. Send me.”

In Jesus Name, Amen

~ Jenna Riggs

For more prayers and encouragement from Jenna, join our Devotionals Space in the TTVN Community!

Until Next Week

Remember: you don't need a title, a law degree, or anyone's permission to get involved. You need awareness, courage, and the resolve to stay in it when others walk away.

True the Vote will keep doing our part. With faith as our foundation and patriots like you standing in the gap, we'll keep pressing for transparency, accountability, and an America we leave stronger than we found it.

Ever onward.

​

Stand With True the Vote

We can't do this without you — and we wouldn't want to.

Thank you for your support!

item.description:
| Read Online​

​

California just passed three laws to protect election records. None of them stopped Saturday.

​

Highlights:

  • Shasta County's shred: What happened to the November 2024 election materials, despite legislation, an open records request, and a pending court hearing.
  • The 22-month clock: Why California's ballot retention deadline matters, and which election records have different rules.
  • Four bills worth watching: California and Congress move to protect election materials—but who gets access, and when?
  • The next deadline is already ticking: What voters can do now to preserve records, demand answers, and document concerns before 2028.
  • How this affects you and what you can do about it

​

Hi Friend,

The shredding company pulled up to 1643 Market Street in Redding at 8:00 a.m. Saturday.

By 11:48 a.m., it was gone. All of it. Eyewitnesses were there, and we have the footage.

Four days earlier, the Registrar of Voters, Clint Curtis, had stopped the shred himself. He opened 10 sealed ballot boxes and found log sheets in seven of them. Under the county's own reading, records like that belong in a separate file, and have a longer retention period. Instead, they were sealed in the boxes with the ballots. One brave witness' footage shows them going into the shred along with everything else.

True the Vote
@TrueTheVote
🎥SHASTA COUNTY: Inside Look of Today’s Ballot (And More) Shredding. Excellent reporting by Shasta Unfiltered’s Elisa Ballard. She asked the city officials what everyone is thinking: “What government codes are you following here?” “No comment.” “I’m just here to observe.”
12:43 AM • Oct 4, 2026
227
Retweets
361
Likes
Read 18 replies
​

A records request was still open. A lawsuit over the requested records had a hearing set for October 6, three days after the shred. The judge wouldn't hear the emergency petition before the truck arrived.

The county's justification comes down to one deadline: 22 months. California Elections Code § 17301 requires sealed ballot packages to be destroyed 22 months after an election unless someone has filed a contest or a criminal case. For November 2024, the 22 months ran out September 5. County Counsel told supervisors that keeping the materials any longer broke the law, and the Secretary of State told the registrar to go ahead.

The trouble is that § 17301 covers sealed ballot packages. It doesn't cover logs, batch sheets or observer sign-in sheets, which all have a longer retention period Those "Tier 2" or "Category 2" materials run on their own retention rules. For some of them, the code says they "may" be destroyed after 22 months, which isn't the same as shall. In Shasta, those records were sitting in the same boxes as the ballots. Our footage shows every one of them going into the truck.

Here's the twist. Just two weeks before the shred, Governor Newsom signed new laws expanding protections for California election records and voting equipment.

California

​SB 1418 — Preservation of Election Materials

  • Issue: Expands protections against removing election materials and certified voting technology from election officials' custody. Also broadens the materials that must be preserved when a qualifying election contest or criminal prosecution is underway.
  • Status: Signed September 19, 2026 (Chapter 341). Urgency statute, effective immediately. Passed the Senate 37–0 on April 27 and Assembly 60–13 on August 20. Senate concurrence passed 30–10 on August 27. Authored by Sen. Sabrina Cervantes.
  • Next Action: None. The law is in effect for the November 3 election.
  • The stake: The law expands preservation requirements when qualifying legal proceedings are underway. But it doesn't eliminate California's existing destruction deadlines. Without an applicable preservation obligation, election materials can still reach the end of their required retention period. Shasta County shows why knowing those deadlines matters.

​AB 1664 — Notice of Warrants and Subpoenas for Election Records

  • Issue: Requires local agencies and election officials to notify California's Secretary of State and Attorney General immediately, but no later than one calendar day, after learning of covered warrants, subpoenas or law enforcement investigations involving the search, seizure or retention of election records or certified voting technology. Authorizes either state office to challenge warrants or subpoenas in court.
  • Status: Signed September 19, 2026 (Chapter 336). Urgency statute, effective immediately. Authored by Assemblymembers Corey Jackson and Marc Berman. Provisions sunset January 1, 2030.
  • Next Action: None. Applies to the November 3 election.
  • The stake: California's top election and law enforcement officials now receive rapid notice of covered investigations involving election materials and can seek court intervention. That could lead to legal challenges over access to records, including those sought by federal investigators. Notification itself does not automatically block a subpoena.

​AB 282 — Felony for Seizing Election Materials Before Certification

  • Issue: Establishes felony penalties for seizing, causing or assisting in the seizure of ballots, election records or certified voting technology before election results are certified, subject to statutory exceptions.
  • Status: Signed September 19, 2026 (Chapter 330). Urgency statute, effective immediately. Authored by Asm. Gail Pellerin, a former Santa Cruz County registrar. Penalties can reach three years for prohibited seizures and four years for certain supervisory directions to seize.
  • Next Action: None. The law is in effect.
  • The stake: California has strengthened criminal penalties for certain seizures before certification. But restricting seizure isn't the same as guaranteeing public access or independent examination. Separate laws still determine how long election materials are preserved and who can inspect them.

Congress

​S. 5124 — SHIELD Our Elections Act

  • Issue: Would restrict state and federal law enforcement from seizing covered federal election records, papers or equipment before recounts, audits and legal challenges are conclusively resolved. A federal judge could authorize seizure upon clear and convincing evidence that the materials are at risk of destruction, subject to joint-custody requirements.
  • Status: Introduced July 23, 2026, by Sen. Alex Padilla with seven cosponsors (six Democrats and one independent). Referred to Senate Rules and Administration. No subsequent committee action identified.
  • Next Action: No hearing or vote scheduled in the records reviewed.
  • The stake: The bill would place additional restrictions on when investigators can seize federal election materials. It includes an exception when destruction is a demonstrated risk, but even then, custody would be shared. Shasta County raises a timely question: how can evidence be preserved and independently examined before destruction deadlines arrive?

Watch the discovery footage here 👇👇👇

True the Vote
@TrueTheVote
🚨 CALIFORNIA: This is happening NOW. 2024 election materials are being pulled from storage ahead of destruction tomorrow. But when the boxes were opened in front of media, they didn’t just contain ballots. ELECTION LOGS WERE INSIDE. Logs that should be preserved for 5 years.
8:28 PM • Oct 2, 2026
5381

9178
Likes
Read 273 replies
​

Shasta County Is the Warning. Your State Is the Assignment.

Saturday's shred took 3 hours and 48 minutes, and the 2024 materials aren't coming back.

Every state has laws governing how election records are stored, who can access them, and when they can be destroyed. And lawmakers across the country are introducing legislation that could change those rules.

Do you know what your state requires?

Head to LegiTrack and start digging. Search for legislation involving election records, ballot retention, audits, public access, and election transparency.

Find out what's already law, what's being proposed, and where your representatives stand.

A new 22-month clock starts November 3. For Shasta and every other county in California, that clock runs out in September 2028. Anything you want to see from this election, you have to request before then, and in writing.

You don't have to live in California for this to matter. If this is happening in a county that the majority of the US hasn't heard of, is it happening in yours?

Filter by your state or federally and use the search bar and type in any number of keywords: record retention, election materials, ballot preservation, destruction of records, public records, seizure of records, chain of custody, etc

Then ask your local election officials the questions that pertain to your area: How long are records kept? Who can inspect them? What happens when someone requests them before they're destroyed?

Don't wait until the shred truck pulls up to find out.

Shasta County is the story today. Making sure it doesn't become your county's story tomorrow? That's where you come in.

Watch the bills. Know the laws. Ask the questions. Get to work.

If you see election records being mishandled, moved or destroyed while a request or case is pending, report it to your county elections office, the Secretary of State or law enforcement when necessary. Then tell us at truethevote.org/helpline. Keep a record of all correspondence, along with times, dates and names.

"Track. Talk. Transform." isn't just a catch phrase. It's essential.

item.title: "Shred everything" was the order.
item.description:
​
​

They Came to Shred Everything. He Brought a Camera.

​

In this newsletter:

  • What Arne List says happened during Shasta County's ballot shredding
  • What was found inside boxes labeled as ballots, and why it matters
  • How "set those aside" reportedly became "shred everything"
  • Why observation is only as powerful as the knowledge behind it...and how every citizen's observation is precious

Hi Friend,

Ten boxes. All marked for destruction. All supposedly ballots.

Seven of them weren't just ballots.

That's what eyewitness Arne List, the voice behind "Where are the ballots?", captured while documenting the first ten boxes opened in Shasta County, California. Election logs and other records were mixed in with the 2024 ballots.

​California Elections Code § 17300 says:

“The elections official shall preserve all rosters or combined rosters and voter lists … until five years after the date of the election, after which they may be destroyed by that official.”

While certain materials have a 22-month retention period, some may have two years, and even up to five. Even then, destruction is discretionary — nothing in the law says they must be destroyed within that time period.

And Arne was standing there when it happened — with his camera rolling.

"Shred Everything."

This week on TTVN Live, Arne walked us through it.

Shasta County Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis has been sounding the alarm about the 2024 ballots for months after several witnesses and whistleblowers came forward.

While he did finally reach federal investigators (and thanks to all of you who helped reach out!), the 2026 ballots are currently the ones under investigation — but the 2024 ballots remained sealed and set for destruction. But when Curtis began opening them, he found the logs and records mixed in.

True the Vote
@TrueTheVote
🚨 CALIFORNIA: This is happening NOW. 2024 election materials are being pulled from storage ahead of destruction tomorrow. But when the boxes were opened in front of media, they didn’t just contain ballots. ELECTION LOGS WERE INSIDE. Logs that should be preserved for 5 years.
8:28 PM • Oct 2, 2026
5334
Retweets
9112
Likes
Read 267 replies
​

At first, the instruction was to set the questionable materials aside.

Then that instruction was reversed.

The new one? Shred everything.

Concerns had been raised and litigation sought preservation, but the shredding went ahead anyway.

Arne witnessed it, and he recorded it.

Arne chronicled the entire day. It shows everything going into the shredder, including the records — not just the ballots.

So now there's more than competing accounts. There are citizens who sought these records via PRAs, footage that can be examined alongside the records, the applicable laws, and the court filings.

He Didn't Need a Title

Arne didn't hold office or have an appointment.

What he had was an understanding of what he was looking at. He knew which questions to ask, and he documented what he could lawfully observe.

As we have said many, many times before: observation is power. But observation paired with knowledge is something else entirely.

Now think about your own county.

How many records get handled every day with no citizen in the room? How many decisions get made and procedures carried out without anyone asking whether the rules are being followed?

How many times have we assumed somebody else was watching?

You Can't Spot What You Don't Understand

For years, we've urged citizens to get involved locally. Become a poll worker. Observe election procedures. Attend county meetings. Learn your state's election laws. Request public records. Ask questions.

Arne's story shows why.

You can't recognize a problem with a process you don't understand. And you can't document something you never showed up to see.

That doesn't mean assuming wrongdoing every time something looks unusual. It means learning the process well enough to tell ordinary procedure from something that deserves a closer look.

When questions come up, document the facts, follow the proper channels, and keep the receipts.

Start With Your County

You don't have to investigate the entire country.

  • Find out who runs your elections and what observation opportunities exist.
  • Read your state's election code, especially its records retention rules.
  • Attend a public meeting.
  • Ask how your county handles election materials.
  • If something concerns you, document it lawfully and accurately.

If this is happening in Shasta County, a county that has — up until recently — remained under the radar, it is happening everywhere. Make no mistake.

One Link in the Chain

Arne was quick to remind us that he's one link in a much larger chain of people working together in Shasta County.

That's what volunteering is.

People have different assignments and different expertise. But every person who shows up makes the effort stronger.

You don't have to do everything. You just have to do something.

​Watch this week's TTVN Live and watch the shredding footage. Share Arne's testimony. Support his legal action. Then ask yourself where your time and talents can make a difference.

Somewhere in America, another set of boxes is waiting to be opened that is scheduled to be destroyed. Another process is running with no one in the room.

Arne brought a camera. What will you bring?

The work isn't glamorous, and it isn't always easy. But it matters.

And so do you.

God bless you, and God bless America.

Ever onward —

Hi Friend,

"It says you're inactive."

Some surprises can wait. That's not one of them.

Here's what else you don't want to find out at the polls:

  • Your address is wrong.
  • Your history shows an election you don't remember voting in, or a way of voting you didn't use.
  • A stranger is registered at your home.
  • Something just doesn't match.

Election Day is the wrong day to start asking why. That's why this week's TTVN Live came down to two words:

Check now.

The reports are flooding in. Here are just some of the reports we've received this week:

One of my registered addresses on file is registered to an address I never lived at because it’s a vacant lot. My wife is also registered there. Scam address!
The third party info shows me as having voted in democrat primaries. I have never voted in a Democrat primary. I became a citizen on 10/18/2006 and was shown as having voted in democratic primaries from 2008 to 2020. I never did that.
My history shows I voted by absentee ballot 11/2/2004. I have NEVER in my voting history ever voted by absentee ballot and I've been registered since I was 18 years old - I'm 57 now.
In the supplemental voting history it says I voted in the Democratic primary 6/11/2002. I have NEVER registered in SC as a Democrat and NEVER voted for any Democrat!
I have never filled out an absentee ballot EVER. Not in 2016 nor 2018!

These reports are not fear mongering, but they are a wake-up call. They also tell a story of how far back this has been occurring.

When you check your record, you are empowered by knowledge. Knowledge is not something those who have been keeping you in the dark want you to have.

Shasta County, CA ROV Clint Curtis joined us again yesterday for an update on the FBI investigation.

Curtis said federal agencies have reviewed materials he provided, though he could not discuss what investigators examined or found. He also described disputes over access to surveillance footage, previously retained ballots and other records, and said he continues to document and refer concerns to the appropriate authorities while pushing for greater transparency in the election process.

But there's a new wrinkle: surveillance footage previously available through public records requests is now being heavily redacted. Curtis says the redactions go beyond obscuring individual employees—the county is now blurring portions of the physical workspace itself, including the staircase and ballot-room area where earlier footage had captured activity that prompted questions. The result: areas the cameras were intended to make observable can no longer be seen in the released footage.

His main call to action was simple: Curtis asked citizens to continue contacting the White House and federal authorities to bring attention to what is happening in Shasta County. He asks that his findings and proposed solutions receive federal review before the midterms.

Scan. Check. Protect. points you to three places:

1. Your registration. Name, address, status, and party where your state records it. Does it all match?

2. Your voting history. Go election by election. If your state shows how you voted, check that too. Voted in person? The record should say in person. See an election you sat out? Take note.

3. Who else is registered at your address. Do you know every name? If one doesn't make sense, don't shrug it off.

Check My Record

item.description:
| Read Online​

​

One rule is dead for November: The fight over when your ballot counts has just started.

​

Highlights:

  • The Supreme Court declined to lift an injunction against the USPS ballot-mail rule, keeping its mandatory barcode, envelope, and voter-data requirements from taking effect for the November 3 midterms. The litigation itself continues.
  • Meanwhile, Congress has three Ballots by Election Day Act bills pending—H.R. 10276, S. 5355, and S. 5001—that would require federal-election ballots to arrive by poll closing time. California also enacted SB 259, creating criminal penalties for certain interference with mail-ballot delivery.
  • For voters: Know your state's deadlines, mail early if using USPS, or use an authorized drop box or other available return method.

​

Hi Friend,

Picture a ballot envelope sitting in a sorting bin in September. It has the right stamp, the right address and a voter's signature.

Under the rule USPS finalized in August, official ballot envelopes would have needed a USPS-compliant barcode, and noncompliant ballot mail could be refused.

That rule is blocked for now. USPS finalized the rule in August, but courts blocked it before it could govern the November 3 election.

Ballots are already moving through the mail while the rules around them keep shifting. The postmark on your envelope may not even show the day you mailed it. The deadline for your ballot to arrive depends on which state you live in.

Here's what happened, and the three bills trying to settle it.

What Just Happened

  • March 31: President Trump signed Executive Order 14399, directing USPS to write new rules for ballot mail in federal elections.
  • June 29: In Watson v. RNC, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that states may count ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive afterward. Justice Barrett wrote the opinion. That kept "grace periods" legal in 14 states and D.C.
  • August 21: USPS released its final rule. States would have to use barcoded official envelopes, give 90 days' notice before using mail voting, and send lists of mail voters to a new federal portal 60 days before an election. Ballots without the barcode could be refused.
  • August 27 and September 13: Two federal judges blocked the rule. Judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts reinstated an order halting it. Judge Carl Nichols in D.C. found USPS went beyond its rulemaking power.
  • September 14: The Supreme Court denied the administration's emergency request in USPS v. California. The rule will not apply to the November 3 midterms. Its long-term future is still being fought in court, including at the First Circuit.

Why this pertains to you

Blocking the rule doesn't resolve the underlying question: who decides when a mailed ballot counts? Congress, the states and the courts are each answering it differently. The quiet problem through all of it is the postmark. Under USPS's postmark rule, the date stamped on your envelope can reflect when the mail was processed, not when you dropped it off. In grace-period states, that date can decide whether your ballot counts.

California

​SB 259: Criminal Penalties for Interfering with Mail Ballots

  • Issue: Makes it a misdemeanor to interfere with a mail ballot's delivery to a voter, and a felony when the person doing it has authority to direct others.
  • Status: Signed September 19, 2026 (Chapter 331). It was an urgency statute, so it took effect immediately. It passed the Assembly on August 28 and the Senate on August 30. It was one of 13 election bills signed the same day — an "election protection" package.
  • Next Action: Effective immediately. The law expressly applies in time for the November 3 general election.
  • Why we're watching: The law was written with the USPS rule in mind and was deliberately accelerated during the final stretch. How those provisions interact with conflicting federal directives, if such a conflict occurs, could become a federalism question for the courts.

​

New Jersey

​S3815: Voter Warning on USPS Postmark Rules

  • Issue: Directs the Secretary of State to run a $100,000 public awareness campaign on how USPS postmark rules could get ballots rejected, and to study where drop boxes are placed.
  • Status: Passed the Senate 30–9 on June 18, 2026. It is now in the Assembly State and Local Government Committee. The identical Assembly bill is A4863.
  • Next Action: No committee hearing date set.
  • Why we're watching: New Jersey law makes the postmark significant for ballots arriving after Election Day. The bill would warn voters that a ballot mailed on Election Day could receive a later postmark, explain how to request a manual postmark, and point voters to drop boxes as an alternative unaffected by USPS postmarking.

​

Congress

​H.R. 10276 / S. 5355 / S. 5001: Ballots by Election Day Act

  • Issue: Amends the Help America Vote Act so ballots in federal elections must be received by the close of polls on Election Day to be counted. Protections for military and overseas voters stay in place.
  • Status: Three versions, all in committee. Sen. Ashley Moody filed S. 5001 on July 15. Sens. James Lankford and Mike Lee filed S. 5355 on August 6. Rep. Laurel Lee filed H.R. 10276 on September 3, and it went to House Administration. The Senate bills went to Rules and Administration.
  • Next Action: No hearing set. The House version would take effect for federal elections starting in 2027.
  • Why we're watching: Watson left the deadline up to each state, and The bills would replace the current state-by-state approach with a federal receipt deadline for federal elections. A single receipt deadline would eliminate post-Election Day receipt windows for covered federal ballots, while leaving the actual canvass and counting process to continue under applicable law.

What you can do before November 3:

  • Mail your ballot early, well before your state's deadline.
  • If you mail close to the deadline, ask the clerk at the counter to hand-cancel it so the postmark shows that day's date.
  • Use a drop box or return it in person if your state allows it.
  • If your ballot is delayed, refused or mishandled, report it to your county elections office or your Secretary of State. Contact law enforcement if it's needed.
  • Then let us know at https://truethevote.org/helpline. Keep a record of every call, email, date, time and name.

That ballot is still sitting in a sorting bin somewhere. It doesn't need a federal barcode this time.

Whether it counts will still come down to two things: the date a machine stamps on it, and the state it's headed to. For now, California, New Jersey and Congress are each giving a different answer.

Check the status of every bill in this issue on LegiTrack, and share this with someone who votes by mail.

Ever onward -

item.title: Can Someone See Which Ballot Was Yours?
item.description:
​
Princeton reconstructed 1.5 million Georgia ballots. We filed September 1.

​

In this newsletter:

  • Catherine's two-part answer to why engage — neither half is about winning
  • The newest Scan. Check. Protect. tools, and the button most people skip
  • Georgia's secret-ballot problem, the Princeton reconstruction, and our September 1 complaint
  • Jenna on the heaviness, and why it isn't a reason to quit

Hi Friend,

Somebody asked why anyone should still be involved after years, the research, and the waiting. She didn't say "because we're going to win."

She said: to bear witness, and to bring hope.

Start with your own record

Vico walked through the newest Scan. Check. Protect. tools. Pull up your registration. Check the participation history. See who else is registered at your address. Then hit the button at the end — green, yellow, or red. That's how we spot the patterns.

Red result? Take it to your county office, tell us, and write down every name, date, and call.

From there, keep telling your story. One story becomes ten.

Your ballot is supposed to be secret

Kevin's segment was a shocking one.

The short version: Georgia's cast vote records are supposed to be scrambled so nobody can match a ballot to a voter. The flaw in that scrambling has been known since 2022. Princeton just used public records and ordinary AI to reconstruct the order of roughly 1.5 million ballots from the May primary.

The question isn't whether someone can see that you voted. It's whether they can pick out which ballot was yours.

We filed a complaint and Georgia's answer so far is: tell counties to restrict and redact what they release. Which also happens to be exactly what citizens use to audit an election.

Listen to his full segment here: https://rumble.com/v7fk620-why-engage-scp-toolkits-and-prayer-episode-24.html​

The heavy part...

Jenna, our "secret treasure" and the author behind TTVN's Daily Devotionals, closed the show in prayer. She named the heaviness a lot of us are carrying, and pointed to Elijah under the tree, David crying out, the disciples in the storm. The storms were real, but so was God's presence in them.

He is the same yesterday, today, and forever. No matter the present storm, He stands with us.

So — why engage?

Not to win. To bear witness, because somebody has to get close enough to see clearly and say so. And to bring hope, because people are watching to see if anyone still thinks this is worth doing.

Check your record. Share the tool. Call your county. Sign up to serve.

Bear witness. Bring hope. Choose in.

“For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.” — Acts 4:20
